title: Loud and Clear: Effective Language of Instruction Policies for Learning
authority: World Bank
claim_supported: In LMICs, an estimated 37% of about one billion students (370 million) are not taught in the language they speak and understand best; 27% speak untaught Minority Written Languages; 220 additional written languages could serve about 270 million students; 559 country-language programs would reach 84% in each country.
unit_of_analysis: aggregate LMIC student population; Ethnologue-derived language and country-language counts
limitations: The report does not print the names of the 220 languages; estimates are preliminary, use 2020 Ethnologue data, treat proficiency too binarily, and require country-level verification. It explicitly excludes tertiary, TVET, adult, and lifelong education.
source_tier: primary institutional synthesis with disclosed secondary data basis

title: All available subjects for our free textbooks
authority: OpenStax, Rice University
claim_supported: OpenStax textbooks are openly licensed, peer reviewed, and designed to standard scope and sequence; the page is the official catalog entry point.
unit_of_analysis: OpenStax title/catalog
limitations: Live catalog changes; the landing page alone does not expose a stable machine-readable title inventory.

title: Free college textbooks, peer-reviewed
authority: OpenStax, Rice University
claim_supported: OpenStax reports 62 college textbooks, eight higher-education subject families, free online and PDF availability for every textbook, accessibility efforts toward WCAG 2.2 AA, and some DAISY/Braille-ready/audio availability.
unit_of_analysis: current higher-education catalog and delivery formats
limitations: Self-reported live figures; title-level accessibility and language availability must be checked individually.

title: Open Logic Project Builds
authority: Open Logic Project
claim_supported: The official build index exposes complete PDFs, modular parts/chapters/sections, and textbook remixes including Sets, Logic, Computation; Incompleteness and Computability; Boxes and Diamonds; Set Theory: An Open Introduction; Intermediate Logic; and What If?.
unit_of_analysis: Open Logic textbook, part, chapter, and section build
limitations: The live index may change; some listed textbooks are drafts and not all modules are pedagogically equivalent.

title: forall x: Calgary—A Free and Open Introduction to Formal Logic
authority: Open Logic Project
claim_supported: A concrete introductory formal-logic curriculum with downloadable print/screen/accessibility-oriented outputs, HTML/source/SCORM options, and named German and Portuguese translations.
unit_of_analysis: introductory formal-logic textbook and format
limitations: Translation and format status must be verified at artifact level; the book is one remix rather than the full Open Logic corpus.

title: GPT-5.6 Sol model documentation
authority: OpenAI
claim_supported: Dated API scenario prices are $4 per million uncached input tokens, $0.40 per million cached input tokens, and $20 per million output tokens; prompts above 272K input tokens are charged at 2x input and 1.5x output for the full request; cache writes are 1.25x uncached input.
unit_of_analysis: API token category and request
limitations: API pricing is not a conversion rule for Codex/ChatGPT weekly-compute allowances. Prices and promotion terms are time-varying; money is a scenario, not the primary compute metric.
locator: model page lines 811-852 in web extraction

title: Organization usage API reference
authority: OpenAI
claim_supported: Official usage fields distinguish total input tokens, cached input tokens, uncached text/image/audio inputs, cache-write tokens, output tokens, and request counts.
unit_of_analysis: organization usage bucket
limitations: Schema availability does not imply that comparable category-level records exist for every local prior task or for a weekly product allowance.
locator: usage reference lines 527-576 in web extraction

title: Licensing information for OpenStax textbooks
authority: OpenStax, Rice University
claim_supported: The official help article describes current OpenStax textbooks as CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and explicitly permits adaptation, remixing, and translation subject to attribution, noncommercial use, and share-alike terms.
unit_of_analysis: OpenStax textbook reuse policy
limitations: Individual titles and third-party components can carry different licenses. Current book web pages also display a separate notice against LLM training or ingestion without permission; AI-assisted adaptation therefore requires title-level rights verification rather than a blanket assumption.

title: Introduction to Computer Science, Chapter 8 Summary—citation and attribution notice
authority: OpenStax, Rice University
claim_supported: A current official OpenStax book page states that the book may not be used to train or otherwise be ingested into large language models or generative-AI offerings without OpenStax permission, while also identifying the book as CC BY-NC-SA.
unit_of_analysis: title-level current web notice
limitations: The notice's interaction with the Creative Commons grant is a legal question this paper does not resolve; it is recorded as an operational permission risk, not as a categorical conclusion about lawful use.

title: Languages in Nepal: National Population and Housing Census 2021 Thematic Report XI
authority: National Statistics Office, Government of Nepal
claim_supported: The 2021 census reports 124 mother tongues and 29,164,578 people. Annex 3 prints exact counts by mother tongue and sex. Tables 4.2 and 4.8 report language-specific literacy and SEE-or-higher attainment for major mother tongues; the report states that instructional medium is mainly Nepali and English in some private schools.
unit_of_analysis: census-reported mother tongue; population age 5+ for literacy; language-specific education attainment
limitations: Census labels such as Tharu and Rai can aggregate varieties. Association with attainment is not a causal language effect and the report explicitly notes socioeconomic and location factors.

title: Population by Mother Tongue, Census of India 2011, C-16
authority: Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India
claim_supported: Official national and state mother-tongue counts for the 22 scheduled-language categories and detailed mother-tongue labels.
unit_of_analysis: census-reported mother tongue
limitations: 2011 is dated; the official Hindi category is an umbrella that cannot be treated as Standard Hindi; several scheduled-language labels aggregate varieties.

title: Table 11: Population by Mother Tongue, National, Census 2023
authority: Pakistan Bureau of Statistics
claim_supported: Exact national mother-tongue counts totaling 240,458,089, including Punjabi 88,915,544; Pashto 43,633,946; Sindhi 34,401,564; Saraiki 28,849,579; Urdu 22,249,307; Balochi 8,117,795; Hindko 5,590,559; and Brahui 2,778,670.
unit_of_analysis: census-reported mother tongue
limitations: Census labels such as Punjabi, Pashto, Balochi, Hindko and Kohistani can aggregate distinct varieties; L2 reach is not included.

title: Population Composition of Nepal: National Population and Housing Census 2021 Thematic Report I
authority: National Statistics Office, Government of Nepal
claim_supported: Annex 10 independently reproduces the national mother-tongue totals used in the language thematic report.
unit_of_analysis: census-reported mother tongue
limitations: Same underlying 2021 census as ACE-E010; useful as an independent official locator, not an independent sample.

title: Mutual intelligibility and communicative functions in Interslavic
authority: Merunka et al.
claim_supported: A developer-led peer-reviewed online study obtained 1,822 valid responses; native Slavic respondents achieved an overall result near 84 percent on a seven-gap written professional-text cloze task, with 315 of 1,766 below the five-of-seven threshold.
unit_of_analysis: self-selected Slavic-language respondents completing a short written cloze task
limitations: Self-selection, uneven country representation, developer authorship, reweighting, and a seven-gap task do not establish sustained mathematical-text comprehension or blanket Slavic coverage.

title: Mutual intelligibility between closely related languages in Europe
authority: Gooskens and van Heuven
claim_supported: A 13,566-participant comparison across 16 national languages and 70 pairs used six functional tests; written comprehension was generally easier than spoken and family means were task dependent.
unit_of_analysis: adult and youth participants in functional spoken and written intelligibility tasks
limitations: Results apply to tested natural-language pairs, not constructed bridge surfaces or untested minority varieties; family averages conceal large pairwise asymmetries.

title: Language policy and medium of instruction in formal education
authority: Stephen L. Walter and Carol Benson
claim_supported: Table 14.2 reports 97 languages with more than 10 million speakers: 52 used in education and 45 not used; their gross populations are 3,380,555,080 and 1,120,220,125. Across all size categories, 3,741,110,588 people are in languages used in education and 2,300,263,716 are in languages not used, yielding 61.9 percent L1 access and 38.1 percent without it. The printed chapter does not expose a named list of the 97 languages.
unit_of_analysis: language-size category and gross population, not named languages or enrolled students
limitations: 2012 aggregate estimates combine published and specialist information; the education-use criterion is broad, the table is not a current census, and its unnamed totals cannot be distributed across modern language candidates. The 38.1 percent is population-weighted, not 45 divided by 97.

title: Zimbabwe 2022 Population and Housing Census Report
authority: Zimbabwe National Statistics Agency (ZIMSTAT)
claim_supported: Table 2.17 prints national mother-tongue counts and provincial distributions, including Shona 11,251,734; Ndebele 1,599,324; Ndau 372,607; Tonga 231,159; Shangani 115,133; Venda 71,647; Kalanga 52,296; Nambya 38,302; and a census label Sign Language 1,620.
unit_of_analysis: census-reported mother tongue within Zimbabwe
limitations: The census labels can aggregate varieties; the Sign Language row does not identify a specific signed language or enumerate all signers; mother-tongue population is not itself an education-access deficit.

title: 2018 Malawi Population and Housing Census Main Report
authority: National Statistical Office of Malawi
claim_supported: Table 3.5 and Appendix Table E3 report self-identified tribe, including Chewa 6,020,945 in the main table, Lomwe 3,302,634, Yao 2,321,763, Ngoni 1,819,347, and Tumbuka 1,614,955. The census questionnaire asked tribe rather than language.
unit_of_analysis: census-reported tribe within Malawi
limitations: These are ethnicity/tribe proxies and must not be relabeled as language-speaker counts. The main and appendix tables differ slightly in a few totals; use only with an explicit proxy label and sensitivity range.
locator: Table 3.5, printed p. 20; Appendix Table E3, printed p. 129

title: C-17: Population by bilingualism and trilingualism, India, 2011
authority: Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India
claim_supported: The national workbook gives each census language category's total speakers and hierarchical counts for first and second subsidiary languages. A reproducible extraction identifies the exact English-or-Hindi union for 122 national categories without double-counting speakers who reported both. Examples: Bengali 14,164,474 of 97,237,669; Telugu 13,878,134 of 81,127,740; Tamil 13,992,609 of 69,026,881; Marathi 36,954,768 of 83,026,680; and Punjabi 17,571,723 of 33,124,726 reported English or Hindi as a subsidiary language.
unit_of_analysis: census language category and reported first/second subsidiary-language knowledge
limitations: Reported language knowledge is not academic reading comfort, and scheduled-language categories can aggregate mother tongues. The extracted union is used as an overlap bound, not as proof that every bilingual speaker can use an advanced English or Hindi textbook.
locator: Sheet1 national rows; columns for total speakers and first/second subsidiary languages

title: Wikipedia Site Statistics tabular dataset
authority: Wikimedia Commons / MediaWiki Siteinfo
claim_supported: The CC0 tabular feed provides current per-project counts derived from MediaWiki Siteinfo. A reproducible extraction yields 369 language/project codes, including 359 active Wikipedia editions, 102 Wikibooks editions with content pages, 20 Wikiversity editions, and 88 Wikisource editions in this snapshot.
unit_of_analysis: Wikimedia project code and site-statistics counter
limitations: Counts measure Wikimedia presence, not advanced mathematics, educational quality, readership, or total language resources. Automated article creation can inflate article totals; activity and article-per-active-user diagnostics must remain visible.

title: World Development Indicators API: access and education context
authority: World Bank
claim_supported: The official API supplies dated country-level values for population, internet use, electricity access, adult literacy, gross secondary enrollment, and gross tertiary enrollment. The preserved snapshot contains 217 countries/territories and 43 World Bank aggregates with indicator-specific observation years.
unit_of_analysis: country or World Bank aggregate and indicator-year
limitations: National averages are not language-specific, community-specific, rural, affordability, disability, device, or service-quality measures. Latest observation years differ, and gross enrollment can exceed 100 percent. Country values support delivery-context sensitivity only.
locator: indicators SP.POP.TOTL, IT.NET.USER.ZS, EG.ELC.ACCS.ZS, SE.ADT.LITR.ZS, SE.SEC.ENRR, and SE.TER.ENRR

title: SONAR language support and FLORES-200 mapping
authority: Meta AI / facebookresearch
claim_supported: The official SONAR README maps 204 FLORES-200 language-script codes to SONAR codes, names, scripts, families, subgroupings, NLLB resource level, and in some cases a benchmark variety. The table therefore provides exact language-script benchmark coverage and an explicit High/Low NLLB resource tier.
unit_of_analysis: FLORES-200 language-script benchmark profile
limitations: Benchmark/encoder support is not evidence of current Codex performance, mathematical terminology, educational usability, source fidelity, or fit to an unlisted variety. Resource level is a model-development category, not a judgment about a language or its speakers.
locator: README language table beginning at line 273 in the preserved snapshot

title: OpenAlex mathematics works grouped by detected language
authority: OpenAlex / OurResearch
claim_supported: Grouping works whose primary topic field is Mathematics (field 26) yields 3,623,001 indexed works, 1,696,951 open-access works, and 23,321 open-access books or book chapters in this snapshot. Language counts expose sharp differences: Indonesian 32,350 open-access mathematics works; Thai 321; Vietnamese 194; Bengali 68; Swahili 23; Tamil 9; Telugu 4; Marathi 3; Urdu 2; and zero for several detected-language groups despite nonzero indexed works.
unit_of_analysis: OpenAlex work classified to primary field Mathematics and detected language
limitations: Language detection and index coverage are uneven; counts include research rather than only teaching material, and zero can mean absent, undetected, or unindexed. This is a bibliographic scarcity proxy, not a direct inventory of usable open textbooks or advanced mathematics in a language.
locator: filters primary_topic.field.id:26, open_access.is_oa:true, and type:book|book-chapter; group_by language

title: Percentage of primary students whose first or home language is a language of instruction
authority: UNESCO Institute for Statistics via World Bank Education Statistics
date: latest available country observation, 2013-2019; snapshot retrieved 2026-08-25
claim_supported: The API exposes 83 latest non-null country observations. Examples include Bangladesh 99.0% (2019), Mongolia 98.0% (2018), Indonesia 43.75487% (2015), Zimbabwe 48.9% (2019), Ghana 12.6% (2018), Gambia 3.2% (2018), and Burkina Faso 0.41156% (2014).
unit_of_analysis: country-level share of primary students, both sexes
limitations: Country observations come from different survey or assessment sources and years. The complement to 100% is country context only: it is not an exact-language deficit, does not identify which communities are mismatched, and cannot be assigned to every speaker of a candidate language.
locator: indicator UIS.FHLANGILP.1; latest non-null observation per country; definition supplied by API metadata

title: The 2010 Population and Housing Census (Whole Kingdom): usual languages spoken at home
authority: National Statistical Office, Thailand
claim_supported: Table 7 reports 59,866,190 people using only Thai at home, 4,214,001 using Thai and other languages, and 1,901,468 using only other languages. Their mutually exclusive Thai-using strata yield a 64,080,191-person Thai-edition ceiling. Named other-language rows include Malay/Yawi 1,467,369, Burmese 827,713, Karen 441,114, Khmer-labelled 180,533, Hmong/Mea 149,090, and Mon 47,298.
unit_of_analysis: 2010 census person by usual language category at home
limitations: The table mixes mutually exclusive Thai-use strata with named other-language categories that can overlap Thai-plus-other users. Several labels are macro categories, transliteration errors, or country names rather than commission-ready varieties. Figures are 2010 observations and some columns differ by one after independent rounding.
locator: Table 7, PDF pp. 98-99; census date on PDF pp. 49-50; visually verified against rendered pages

title: Source-audited literature evidence corpus for marginal educational access per compute
authority: Row-specific peer-reviewed articles, primary institutional reports, and official accessibility standards listed in ACE-A069
claim_supported: Thirty-seven row-level sources characterize language-of-instruction effects and prevalence, structured-pedagogy bundles, OER access mechanisms, translation and AI evidence, digital accessibility standards, and implementation costs. The corrected corpus distinguishes study outcomes from model assumptions and records adverse as well as positive findings.
unit_of_analysis: one peer-reviewed study, official report, or technical standard per evidence row
limitations: The studies use heterogeneous populations, outcomes, and designs. Their coefficients are not universal reach multipliers; every quantitative use must retain its own population, outcome, design, and setting.
source_tier: mixed primary literature and official standards, individually identified in the table
locator: 37 unique record_id values; corrections and artifact hashes in ACE-A072

title: Census 2022 in Brief: language most often spoken in the household
authority: Statistics South Africa
claim_supported: Table 3.8 reports 59,876,448 coded residents aged 1+ across household-language categories. Exact large rows include isiZulu 14,613,202, IsiXhosa 9,786,928, Afrikaans 6,365,488, Sepedi 5,972,255, English 5,228,301, and Setswana 4,972,787. The five nonofficial/context categories sum to 1,247,275.
unit_of_analysis: resident aged 1+ by one language most often spoken with household members
limitations: Not mother tongue, total speakers, literacy, academic comfort, or marginal reach. The generic Sign language row does not identify SASL. Multilingual beneficiary overlap remains unmeasured.

title: Census 2022 Statistical Release (P0301.4)
authority: Statistics South Africa
claim_supported: Table 2.8 provides an official percentage-distribution cross-check for the Census 2022 household-language categories.
unit_of_analysis: percentage distribution by language most often spoken in the household
limitations: Mostly one-decimal shares, with Sign language at 0.02%; use ACE-E027 for exact counts.
source_tier: primary official national census statistical release

title: Cultural Dynamics in South Africa
authority: Statistics South Africa
claim_supported: The thematic report supplies official household-language context and notes possible under-enumeration; its printed nonofficial-category total is 1,252,633.
unit_of_analysis: Census 2022 language profiles and thematic categories
limitations: Its nonofficial-category counts differ from the 1,247,275 total in ACE-E027. Preserve the source-specific observations; do not present them as identical corroboration or silently choose one.
locator: Figure 2.1, printed p. 5; Table 2.4, printed pp. 11-12

title: The Status of the Language of Learning and Teaching in Schools: A Quantitative Overview, 2008-2016
authority: South Africa Department of Basic Education
claim_supported: For 2016, the report supplies language-specific counts of learners whose school LoLT did or did not match reported home language. Foundation Phase totals are 2,402,540 matches and 540,484 nonmatches; Intermediate Phase totals are 585,808 matches and 1,844,086 nonmatches.
unit_of_analysis: registered learner by home language and whether the school offers a matching LoLT, within one education phase
limitations: Principal-reported Annual School Survey/EMIS data have explicit verification and consistency warnings. They are historical school-level correspondence, not direct classroom language, comprehension, or a share that may be multiplied by 2022 census counts.
locator: methods/data cautions printed pp. 16-17; Figures 9 and 11 and Tables 7 and 8, printed pp. 31-34

title: Pinned OpenStax and Open Logic workload denominators
authority: Exact local source files and hash-verified Open Logic source closure
claim_supported: Independent remeasurement verified 257 available OpenStax modules totaling 1,017,337 visible ASCII-alpha source tokens and every one of 722 Open Logic source units totaling 367,220 tokens. FR-2 is exactly 210 units and 120,083 tokens. All 60 portfolio-compute calculations reproduce their inputs.
unit_of_analysis: hash-pinned source module or Open Logic source unit
limitations: Four additional OpenStax books have exact module counts but only planning token intervals; OpenStax XML and Open Logic TeX preprocessing differ; compute factors are scenarios rather than observed model usage.

title: Direct-language and proxy observations for large Asian evidence gaps
authority: National statistical offices, census publications, and authoritative survey/census-program records individually registered in ACE-A110
claim_supported: The frozen package contains 109 observations: 46 direct-language populations, two population-wide proficiency measures, 18 sample-case frequencies, and 43 ethnicity proxies. Thirty-four direct-language rows pass its strict staging rule. Exact large direct observations include Khmer mother tongue 14,893,134 (Cambodia 2019), Turkmen mother tongue 6,297,965 (Turkmenistan 2022), and Kyrgyz native language 5,527,168 (Kyrgyzstan 2022).
unit_of_analysis: one source-reported language, proficiency, sample-case, or ethnic-proxy category with its original measure
limitations: No direct census-scale Bangla, Vietnamese, Burmese, Lao, or Mongolian language population was found in this package. Ethnicity is never converted to language. Kazakhstan native-language values are nationality-scoped lower bounds; Uzbekistan is preliminary and rounded.
source_tier: mixed primary official and authoritative program evidence, row-specific

title: African exact census cells and weighted adult home-language shares
authority: National statistical offices and Afrobarometer sources individually registered in ACE-A113
claim_supported: The frozen package contains 43 language observations across 11 territories. Exact person-count examples include Bambara/Bamanankan mother tongue 9,551,561 in Mali's 2022 census and Wolof principal language 8,786,892 in Senegal's 2023 census. Twenty-eight Afrobarometer rows are weighted adult response shares and remain contextual rather than population counts.
unit_of_analysis: source-specific census person count, literacy cell, nonexclusive prevalence share, or weighted adult language-response share
limitations: Rwanda and Burundi literacy rows are nested alternatives; Morocco Amazigh profiles are nonexclusive; survey shares have no design-correct interval here and cannot be ranked as people without a separately sourced denominator.
source_tier: mixed primary official census and authoritative probability-survey evidence, row-specific
locator: ACE-A113 through ACE-A116; central validation ACE-A121

title: Exact residual-language observations in the Americas, Oceania, and Europe
authority: U.S. Census Bureau, Australian Bureau of Statistics, and Statistics Poland sources registered in ACE-A117
claim_supported: The package preserves 55 exact language rows: 35 ACS age-5-plus home-language estimates with published 90 percent margins of error, 10 Australian census home-language counts, and 10 Polish multiple-response home-language counts. Examples include Navajo 161,200 [158,202, 164,198] in the United States, Kriol 7,478 in Australia, and Silesian 467,145 in Poland.
unit_of_analysis: one territory-specific direct language observation in the source's stated population universe
limitations: Counts are territory-specific, not global language populations. Polish rows overlap because respondents may report multiple languages. The sources do not establish scripts, orthographies, educational mismatch, or academic-language comfort.
locator: ACE-A117 through ACE-A120; central validation ACE-A121

title: Evidence-bounded interlanguage, shared-core, and accessibility mechanism matrix
authority: Registered local edition inventories, direct Interslavic study evidence, natural-language intelligibility literature, official population observations, and exact compute denominators indexed in ACE-A126
claim_supported: The 104-row matrix distinguishes one-surface constructed bridges from named localized outputs that reuse a semantic/formula core, script derivatives, scaffolds, and accessibility formats. None of the 113 population links is usable as a package total. The Interslavic pooled 0.84 short-cloze score is retained once as study evidence and is never copied to language leaves or multiplied by a Slavic population ceiling.
unit_of_analysis: one exact intervention-output/community edge
limitations: Most cross-language mathematical comprehension increments are unmeasured. Localized-output identity is conditional on literacy and does not by itself measure educational exclusion.
source_tier: mixed direct study, primary official population, and reproducible local artifact evidence

title: Observed named-output population and compute comparison for shared-core packages
authority: Centrally validated population links and FR-2 token scenarios, with reuse fractions explicitly labeled unobserved
claim_supported: In the base-token/base-reuse view, Punjabi Gurmukhi plus Shahmukhi has 120,059,639 exact named-population observations and 6,109,574 modeled gross tokens; the two new Urdu outputs in the Hindi-Urdu shared-register package have 72,975,069 and the same modeled tokens. Other observed-gross partial or complete package sums are Indonesian/Malay 42,682,566, Nguni 27,137,226, Turkic 25,452,562, Sotho-Tswana 15,624,006, Manding 9,551,561, and the Germanic hypothesis 6,365,488. Constructed Interslavic receives zero conservative demographic reach.
unit_of_analysis: one named-output package under one token and reuse sensitivity scenario
limitations: Territory language observations are gross ceilings for usable access and may omit other territories. Reuse fractions are unobserved, some target profiles lack marginal-factor joins, and the result is not the final deduplicated recommendation ranking.
source_tier: reproducible derived analysis from exact registered inputs

title: Authoritative secondary person estimates for major Asian language-population gaps
authority: Unicode CLDR 48.2, a peer-reviewed Vietnamese-language source, CLEAR/IPUMS Philippines extract, archived CIA estimates republished by the Netherlands Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the World Bank denominator, all registered in ACE-A136
claim_supported: Fifteen person observations fill gaps that lacked stronger direct national language counts. Source-reported or derived bases include Bangladesh Bangla 165,323,060 functional users, Vietnamese over-89-million lower bound, Burmese 36,817,344 functional users, Dari 30,083,114 overlapping total speakers, Cebuano 20,697,364 weighted main-language persons, Sinhala 14,948,168 functional users, and Tajik 10,394,100 functional users. Stronger direct Uzbek evidence is retained instead, and Tagalog is not mapped to Filipino.
unit_of_analysis: one named language and territory under the source's exact functional-user, speaker, or weighted-person measure
limitations: Most sources publish no numerical interval or component vintage. Functional-user totals are ceilings rather than mother-tongue counts; Dari/Pashto overlap; Philippine estimates are 2010 weighted persons; Malaysian Malay is context only pending standard-variety fit.
source_tier: row-specific authoritative secondary or transparent derived evidence

title: Source-audited scripts, orthographies, standards, and split decisions for previously unresolved target profiles
authority: Official language/orthography authorities, statutory and community education sources, IANA/CLDR identifiers, institutional language resources, and exact population authorities indexed in ACE-A154
claim_supported: All 55 previously unresolved score rows received an explicit profile decision. Thirty-nine have a single valid BCP 47 profile, three have multiple valid localized profiles, eleven have valid base tags that require community or orthographic localization, and Eastern Keres and Tewa remain deliberately unrankable as one edition because the census labels require Pueblo-specific splits. Polish, German, Ukrainian, and Czech are retained as richly served negative controls.
unit_of_analysis: one source population observation and its defensible edition-profile decision
limitations: A registered identifier does not establish literacy or universal community acceptance. Fourteen interventions need split/localized outputs and none of the population counts is a global or direct-literacy audience.
source_tier: row-specific official, community, institutional, or scholarly profile evidence

title: Bounded accessibility populations, mechanisms, residual-overlap rules, and non-rankability result
authority: Official census tables, ITU and WHO context, W3C and DAISY/BANA standards, and official OpenStax/Open Logic accessibility documentation indexed in ACE-A165
claim_supported: The recovered lane contains 15 registered sources, 13 population strata, and 11 intervention edges. Exact ceilings include 771,288 India census respondents age 5-19 in the source visual-disability category who were attending education, 257,755 in the historical cognitive proxy category attending education, NZSL 24,676-24,680, Scotland BSL ability 117,250-117,349, and Peruvian Sign Language childhood-language 10,447. Every intervention remains rank_ready=false because incremental residual gain is unmeasured.
unit_of_analysis: one barrier-specific accessibility intervention and its exact source stratum
limitations: Disability, offline, and signed-language counts are not newly served populations. Existing OpenStax and Open Logic accessibility features reduce marginal reach; strata overlap and cannot be added.
source_tier: primary official demographic and technical-standard evidence

title: Independent strict deduplicated selector audit and reproducible exposure ordering
authority: Independent deterministic audit of registered natural scores, package scores, profile statuses, accessibility return, and model specifications
claim_supported: The strict snapshot contains 83 cardinal interventions: 105 natural score rows minus four controls and 16 unresolved profiles, followed by four exact constituent rows replaced by IL-HU and IL-PUNJABI and two packages added. All 83 conservative floors equal zero. The informative round-robin Top 10 begins Indian Bengali, Bangladesh Bangla, Telugu, Marathi, Punjabi synchronized two-script package, Javanese, Indian Tamil, Vietnamese, Gujarati, and Kannada.
unit_of_analysis: one deduplicated FR-2 linguistic intervention under conservative, base, optimistic, and scarcity views
limitations: The 83-row result is an interim strict snapshot, not the final Top 100. Base access and reuse remain disclosed sensitivities; accessibility has no cardinal scores.
source_tier: reproducible independent model and arithmetic audit

title: Exact production-profile recovery for sixteen formerly unresolved U.S. census-language rows
authority: Official, statutory, tribal, educational, dictionary, IANA/CLDR, and institutional sources frozen in the task-local manifest
claim_supported: Thirteen interventions are now reproducible production units: ten single editions and three two-output bundles. Their source population intervals remain pooled nonadditive ceilings and are never multiplied by output count. Eastern Keres, Tewa, and Guyanese Creole English remain non-rankable exact-profile blockers.
unit_of_analysis: one census population observation and one exact single-edition or enumerated localized-output production unit
limitations: Several exact editions reach only an unknown subset of a broader pooled census cell; the count is an upper ceiling, not an audience-share estimate.
source_tier: row-specific primary or institutional profile evidence plus exact registered population evidence

title: Globally balanced exact-candidate expansion and same-schema sensitivity scores
authority: Registered official census/administrative population observations, IANA identifiers, frozen local context datasets, and the common FR-2 compute model
claim_supported: Thirty-seven disjoint candidate rows add coverage across Asia, Africa, the Americas, Oceania, and Europe. Thirty-five enter the same labelled access-sensitivity model; Pakistani Pashto and Oromo remain D0 mismatches with blank score and rank fields. Expansion IDs and population observations do not overlap the original 105 scores.
unit_of_analysis: one exact language-script-territory proposal and one registered population observation
limitations: Most base access values still use country literacy proxies and a neutral 0.5 academic-nonoverlap sensitivity; they are not measured marginal beneficiaries. Some production profiles remain medium-confidence commissioning specifications rather than claims of universal orthographic acceptance.
source_tier: official person-count observations with explicit source-specific profile and uncertainty controls

title: South African official-language curriculum and orthography evidence
authority: South African Department of Basic Education
date: CAPS policy effective 2012; examination guidance 2015; pages accessed 2026-08-25
claim_supported: The national curriculum provides named Home Language and Mathematics materials for isiNdebele, isiXhosa, isiZulu, Sepedi, Sesotho, Setswana, Siswati, Tshivenda, and Xitsonga. Official examination guidance distinguishes the conjunctive Nguni orthographies from the disjunctive Sepedi/Sesotho/Setswana orthographies and requires standard language.
